editorial.headline: Private Libraries: Nationally Open, but Closed to PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Private-library work is nationally open to full foreign ownership, but Bali’s permanent risk-based moratorium blocks PMA registration there.
editorial.body:
**Private library activity** covers the private-sector management, care, preservation and appraisal of libraries. It is undertaken by non-government parties: individuals, organisations, companies, foundations and other private institutions. The defining boundary is institutional rather than cultural: the library is not under the auspices of an educational institution or another cultural institution.

The work can be as physical or as digital as the collection requires. It includes documentation and information services for private libraries, including digital libraries, reading rooms, listening rooms and viewing rooms. It also encompasses organising both specialist and general collections; cataloguing them; lending and storing books, maps, periodicals, films, recordings, tapes and works of art; and retrieving library documents to meet information needs. Private archive-management activity and private library activity are expressly within this scope.

This is an activity for private operators of varied forms and sizes, from an individual or foundation to an organisation or company. The registration frame is open across Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales. That breadth matters because the activity is not confined to a single format of collection or institution: its scope reaches the systems that make a private collection usable, searchable, maintained and available to its audience.

Nationally, the activity is TERBUKA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. That is the national position. In Bali, however, a foreigner cannot register this activity through PMA today. At the Besar scale, every scope is assessed as Rendah or Menengah-Rendah risk; Bali’s island-wide, permanent moratorium blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA. The Bali outcome is therefore not a reduced foreign-ownership percentage, but a block on PMA registration for this activity despite its nationally open status.
